description: Plays one MPX part on a modelled cello: four strings bowed through a model of rosin's friction, on one bridge and one body, each note's bowing worked out ahead of it.

params.name: Vibrato
params.text: How wide the vibrato is, as a share of each note's own width: at the middle, each note's own — wider on long and loud notes, none on open strings or where the part says senza vibrato, narrower in earlier music; at the bottom, none; at the top, twice as wide. A change is heard at once, on the notes already sounding.

inputs.name: MPX note
inputs.text: One part, played on the cello: its notes, from mpxScore or any MPX source. From a score each note is announced ahead, and its start is worked out before it sounds.

outputs.name: Out
outputs.text: The cello, in mono, as loud as mpxPiano playing the same markings. A single note at fff peaks about 2.7V.

lights.name: Level
lights.text: Flashes green as each note begins, lights orange when the output passes 7.07V, 3 dB under clipping, and red when it reaches 10V, where Rack's audio interface clips.

notes: From a score, each note is announced to the module three seconds before it sounds, and ways of starting it are tried on a copy of the cello while the music plays. A note from a keyboard or a generator, which nothing announced, is played as it arrives, started the way found best for the nearest note like it.
A chord is played as its top note.

Fidelity, in the right-click menu, sets how much is tried on a copy of the cello before each note sounds. Level 1 tries up to eighteen ways of starting each note from the string, and each bow change three ways. Level 2 tries two ways of starting, a short glide and one bite. Level 3, the default, plays one bite without trying it and still tries each bow change. Level 4 tries nothing: each note is played as it arrives, so notes need not be announced ahead, and no second copy of the cello is worked out, for the least computing.

Economy, in the right-click menu, is for less computing at less fidelity: the strings are worked out at half the rate, and a string nobody is playing stops once it has rung down, so it no longer rings in sympathy with the others. It takes about half the computing.
